title: Five Days in the West
subtitle: El blog de viajes de Lucía: Dublín, Galway y una cena con la familia de Daniel

paragraphs: Hello again, everyone! It's been a long time since my last post. I've been working incredibly hard since January, and I just haven't had the energy to write. But last week I finally had a proper holiday, and I want to tell you all about it. Daniel and I spent five days in Ireland: two in Dublin and three in Galway, where his family lives. If you're thinking of visiting Ireland this year, keep reading. I'll tell you what went well, what went wrong and what I'll do differently next time.

Our trip didn't start well. We had an early flight, but we set off late because Daniel couldn't find his passport. Then there was an accident on the motorway, and the traffic was terrible. Daniel kept checking the time on his phone, and I kept saying, "We'll be fine, we'll be fine." We made it to the check-in desk with about two minutes to spare, completely out of breath. Then the agent told me that my suitcase was too heavy and charged me thirty pounds. And after all that running, our flight was delayed by thirty minutes! We spent the extra time in the departure lounge, eating overpriced sandwiches and laughing at ourselves.

Dublin is a small capital, and you can walk almost everywhere. Our hotel, the Liffey House, was right in the centre, a few minutes from the river. The staff were friendly and the breakfast was excellent, but there was one problem: our room faced the street. On a Friday night in Dublin, that means people singing under your window until three in the morning. I'm a light sleeper, so I didn't sleep much. And when I got up, exhausted, there was no hot water in the shower.

I went down to reception, and I tried to stay calm. "I'm sorry to bother you," I said, "but I'm afraid there's a problem with our room." I explained about the noise and the shower. The receptionist couldn't have been nicer. She apologised, sent someone to look at the shower, took ten percent off our bill and offered us a free breakfast. Daniel was delighted about the breakfast, of course. My advice is simple: if you have a problem in a hotel, be polite but clear. It works much better than shouting, and you might even get a free breakfast.

In two days we were able to see a lot. We visited Trinity College, where the old library is one of the most beautiful rooms I have ever seen. Thousands of old books are kept there, on wooden shelves that go all the way up to the ceiling. Photos are allowed, but you have to be quiet, and it's surprisingly hard not to say "wow" every few seconds. We also walked along the river, crossed the famous Ha'penny Bridge and had lunch at a food market. In the evening Daniel took me to a traditional pub with live music. I'm not very good at dancing in public, but after an hour everyone was dancing, including me.

On our third day we took the train across the country to Galway. The journey takes about two and a half hours, and the views are lovely: green fields, stone walls, sheep, cows and more sheep. Daniel used to take this train every Friday when he was a student in Dublin. "I would always sit on the left," he told me, "because you get the best view of the river when the train leaves the city." So, of course, we sat on the left. He would also buy a cup of terrible tea from the trolley, he said, just because it was a tradition. We bought two cups. He was right: it was terrible.

Galway is much smaller than Dublin, but it's full of life. The streets in the old town are painted in bright colours, and there are musicians on almost every corner. It rains a lot. Daniel says it has been raining in Galway since about 1850, and I'm starting to believe him. But nobody seems to mind. People just put on their raincoats and carry on with their day. After a while, I stopped noticing the rain too. Well, almost.

The most important part of the trip, of course, was meeting Daniel's family. I was really nervous. I had a little speech ready in my head, and I practised it again and again on the train. But when Maureen, Daniel's mam, opened the door, she just gave me an enormous hug and said, "You must be Lucía! Come in, come in, you're soaked!" I forgot my speech completely, and I didn't need it.

Maureen had made enough food for twenty people: soup, roast lamb, potatoes cooked in three different ways and a mountain of vegetables. "Have some more potatoes, love," she kept saying. "If you don't eat, I'll be offended!" I told her that if I ate any more, I wouldn't be able to move, and everyone laughed. Halfway through the evening I realised something: I was understanding almost everything. When I arrived in Bristol, I couldn't follow a conversation in a noisy room. Now I was sitting at a crowded Irish table, with the rain hitting the windows, and I was laughing at the jokes. Most of them, anyway. The Galway accent is still a challenge!

The next day the rain stopped for a few hours, so Daniel drove us to the Cliffs of Moher, about an hour and a half from Galway. I've seen a lot of beautiful places, but nothing like this. The cliffs are more than two hundred metres high, and the wind was so strong that we could hardly stand. We stood there in silence for a long time, looking at the Atlantic. Then it started raining again, and we ran back to the car, soaked and laughing. That evening, as soon as we got back, Daniel put the kettle on and Maureen brought out her famous apple tart. I have no words. Just go to Galway and ask for it.

So, here are my tips if you're travelling to the west of Ireland. First, bring a raincoat. Then bring another one. Second, book your train tickets online, because they're much cheaper. Third, don't plan every minute: the best moments of our trip weren't in any guidebook. And finally, learn one word of Irish: sláinte, which means "cheers". Say it in a pub and you'll make friends immediately.

We're flying back to Bristol tomorrow morning, and this time we're leaving for the airport three hours early. Next month I'll be working on a big project at the studio, so I probably won't be posting for a while. But as soon as I have some news, I'll share it here. Thanks for reading, and see you soon! Lucía

questions.question: Why did Lucía stop writing her blog for a while?
options: She was working very hard and had no energy.
She was travelling around Ireland.
Her laptop was broken.

questions.question: What happened at the airport?
options: They missed the flight and took the next one.
They checked in just in time, but she had to pay for her heavy suitcase.
Their flight was cancelled because of the traffic.

questions.question: How did the hotel solve Lucía's complaint?
options: By moving them to a quieter room.
By giving them their money back.
With a discount, a free breakfast and someone to look at the shower.

questions.question: Why did Daniel and Lucía sit on the left side of the train?
options: Daniel always did it as a student, to see the river.
The seats on the right were taken.
The tea trolley only went down the left side.

questions.question: In paragraph 7, "carry on with their day" means…
options: go back home.
continue doing what they were doing.
carry heavy bags.

questions.question: What surprised Lucía during the dinner in Galway?
options: That Maureen didn't speak to her.
That the family didn't eat potatoes.
How much of the conversation she could understand.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of the last two paragraphs?
options: To give advice and say what she will do next.
To complain about the Irish weather.
To describe the history of Galway.

exam_practice.title: Uso del inglés · Una palabra por hueco
exam_practice.instructions: Como en los exámenes oficiales: escribe una sola palabra en cada hueco.

items.text: Lucía hasn't written on her blog ___ January, because she has ___ working very hard. Last week she and Daniel flew to Dublin, ___ they stayed for two nights.
items.hint: Since + punto de partida. Has been + -ing para algo que dura hasta ahora.

items.text: The old library at Trinity College is one ___ the most beautiful rooms she has ever seen. Thousands of books ___ kept there. In Galway, it ___ been raining "since 1850", Daniel jokes.
Daniel ___ to take the train to Galway every Friday. He ___ always sit on the left. ___ they arrived, Maureen gave Lucía a hug, ___ she forgot her speech.
items.hint: Hábitos del pasado: used to y would. So introduce un resultado.

exam_practice.title: Uso del inglés · Forma correcta
exam_practice.instructions: Escribe la forma correcta de la palabra entre paréntesis. Puede hacer falta más de una palabra.

items.text: They ___ (set off) late because Daniel ___ (not / can) find his passport. The flight ___ (delay) by thirty minutes.
items.hint: Set off es irregular (set → set). Can en pasado: could.

items.text: "I'm sorry ___ (bother) you, but there's a problem with our room." "Would you mind ___ (send) someone to look at the shower?"
So far Lucía ___ (visit) two Irish cities. She ___ (go) to the Cliffs of Moher on her last day. If you eat any more, you ___ (not / be able to) move!
items.hint: Hasta ahora (so far): present perfect. Momento terminado (her last day): past simple.

items.text: Next month Lucía ___ (work) on a big project, so she won't be posting much. As soon as she ___ (have) news, she'll share it.
items.hint: Acción en curso en el futuro: will be + -ing. Tras as soon as, presente.
